Flood Insurance Data

Flood zone AE: what it means, who must insure, what it costs

Zone AE is a high-risk area: land with a 1 percent or greater chance of flooding in any given year, where FEMA has worked out how high the water from that flood would reach (44 CFR §59.1, §64.3). A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Must I buy? Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

What have NFIP claims in zone AE paid?

NFIP claims rated AE on every building type (homes, condo buildings, businesses), losses in 2016–2025: 350,668 claims, 288,481 paid, $24,236,353,299 paid in total, $84,014 on average per paid claim across all those buildings, not what a single home gets.

Zone as rated on each claim, not today's map; dollars as paid, not adjusted for inflation. A count of claims is not a chance of flooding for any one home.

How zone AE compares

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards.

Buying, refinancing or questioning the zone

Buying a finished home with an NFIP building policy: the seller can assign the policy to you in writing when title transfers. A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records.

An owner or renter who believes the property was put in a high-risk A or V zone by mistake, because of how the zone line was drawn against streets or other features, can send FEMA technical information and ask for a Letter of Map Amendment, which identifies the property to be excluded from the zone (44 CFR part 70). If you think a lender's high-risk-zone finding is wrong, you and the lender together can ask FEMA to review it within 45 days of the lender's notice; a fee applies (44 CFR §65.17).

In zones AE, AH and VE, FEMA has worked out the water surface elevation of the base flood: the flood level that has a 1 percent or greater chance of occurrence in any given year (44 CFR §59.1, §64.3).

Federal flood insurance (NFIP) is sold only in communities that take part in the NFIP; in a community that has not joined, or once a suspension takes effect, no one can buy an NFIP policy.

Will it rise, and can I pay less?

FEMA prices each building from where it is (distance to the coast, rivers and other flood sources, and how high the ground sits), how it is built (foundation type, first-floor height) and what the policy covers (coverage amounts and deductibles).

By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year; the rate for some property, including homes that are not a primary residence and business property, rises 25% a year until that group's average rate reaches the level the law sets (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)). FloodSmart puts the limit at 18 to 25% a year for most policyholders. It usually does not apply to new policies, raising your coverage or lowering your deductible can go past it, and fees and surcharges are added on top.

FEMA's ways that may lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

How do I get covered?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

What this page cannot tell you

Your premium, private insurers' prices, your exact zone, why prices rise, and FEMA's map and an agent's quote answer those for your address.
